html:
A Babylonian clay tablet from around 1800 BCE, probably from the city of Larsa in southern Iraq, that lists sets of numbers linked to the sides of right triangles. It shows that Babylonian scribes worked with what we call Pythagorean triples more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

The tablet has fifteen rows written in cuneiform numerals in base 60, the system that still gives us 60 minutes in an hour. The columns pair numbers such as 119 and 169, which with 120 make the sides of a right triangle, the relation later known as the Pythagorean theorem. The New York publisher George Plimpton bought it from a dealer around 1922 and left it to Columbia University.

Why it was made is debated. Most historians of Babylonian mathematics think it was a teacher's aid for setting problems; a few have read it as an early table of trigonometry. It dates from the time of the Old Babylonian kingdom, when scribal schools flourished.
